Reckless Driving Hotline

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Reckless Drivers Beware! Little Brothers are watching you! The COJ has launched a Reckless Driving Hotline for residents to send video reports of incidents of bad driving, direct to the JMPD.

Unique Selling Point:
Next time you spot reckless driving on the road don’t you wish you could do something about it? The City of Joburg is giving this opportunity to Johannesburg residents with their new Hotline number for reporting reckless drivers on WhatsApp. But how much safer will our roads be if good citizen drivers are trying to react instantly on their phones to any case of bad driving?

Summary:
Just in February this year, the JMPD managed to catch 541 drunk drivers, but is that just the tip of the iceberg? The City of Joburg certainly think so and Mayor Herman Mashaba launched a new scheme at the end of March to combat driving offences. This time the strategy is to involve Johannesburg citizens, drivers and pedestrians, in alerting the police to road related offences. In essence, the city has set up a “Reckless Driving Hotline” on WhatsApp, the Facebook owned messaging service.

Further information:
“When you see reckless driving behaviour: STOP, move to the side then record or take a picture.” So tweeted @CityofJoburgZA on 27th March this year. The City of Joburg, the Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department and the Department of Community Safety have joined forces in a new anti-road-crime initiative which harnesses the immediacy of video over WhatsApp. They envisage, that on witnessing a dangerous driving incident, vigilant onlookers will take a video of the action, or copy a clip from their car’s dashcam, and send it to 081 470 6338.

Many of us wish we could do something about road crimes, road rage being rife in Johannesburg. But how easy will it be to report to this hotline properly and safely? And how effective will the City act on the alerts?

Carte Blanche looks at how practical it is for a witness of reckless behaviour on the roads to report such incidents to the Hotline. We will do our own demo test to show how practical or impractical the whole process is of pulling over in a safe place, taking a video and then sending it on WhatsApp.

The JMPD in co-operation with the Department of Community Safety have developed a system for receiving the public’s alerts, reviewing them and reacting to those that provide enough information to follow up on. Michael Sun, MMC of The Department of Community Safety, will take us behind the scenes to the operation room and show us how it works. And we will go driving with JMPD spokesperson Wayne Minaar to view the project from the law enforcement perspective.

The JMPD say that on successfully identifying the perpetrator of any such alert by the public, and deeming the incident serious enough to be unlawful, they will issue a traffic citation which will probably include a fine. If multiple crimes are detected in this manner do the courts have capacity for people who don’t come forward to pay the fines? With the backlog in an already overburdened justice system will these traffic offences ever be prosecuted?

The Hotline scheme may also lead to other unwanted side-effects. Ironically, there is the potential for an increase in reckless behaviour on the roads… by people attempting to catch an offender in a haphazard or over-zealous way.

There are also opportunities for malicious exploitation of the scheme. For instance, what if someone holding a grudge towards a neighbour or work colleague, decides to stalk that person with their dashcam or phone at the ready? Then proceed to repeatedly report them to the Hotline for any vaguely reckless behaviour they exhibit on the road?

Even so, however impractical the reporting procedure may be, Cllr Michael Sun emphasises that one of the main ambitions for the project is that,i there are some successful prosecutions and drivers know someone may be watching them, then the Hotline could act as an effective deterrent to reckless driving.

Press Release:


Reckless Driving Hotline
With South African drivers amongst the worst in the world and soaring annual road deaths – would you send videos of bad driving incidents to a police hotline? The City of Johannesburg has set up a WhatsApp group, allowing motorists and pedestrians to do just that. With the click of a button, videos can be sent directly to the metro police department to help them clamp down on reckless driving. Carte Blanche asks: Could this empower frustrated motorists or encourage road rage and vigilantism?
Producer: Sophia Phirippides
Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


Sophia: Follow him.., saying go go go… look at him look at him, look at him… He went across like three lanes did you see that?

Speeded up traffic… beat… lots of cars… or driving shots… people committing traffic offenses off the dash cam footage...

LINK: F*** sakes. Bloody idiot. Doesn’t it drive you crazy when you see reckless dangerous driving right in front of you. Not a cop in sight and you can’t do a thing about it. Well according to the city of Joburg, now you can.

Sound up: Just between Marlborough going over the bridge…

VO: A new Hotline number for reporting reckless drivers on WhatsApp, sends your complaints to the Johannesburg Metro Police Department’s Response Centre. Superintendent Marie Hay is heading up the operation.

Marie: The person will send in a video or a photo, we will look at that, an operator will see what the incident is he will then automate a response to that you will be furnished with a reference number if its an emergency it will be logged on the emergency system which will go immediately to dispatch. Anything that needs investigation goes to our superintendent that’s been assigned to this project.

VO: Law breaking motorists will be issued with a citation and either have to pay a fine or appear in court.

Derek: What do you need from the person sending the submission

Marie:The location is very important.

Marie: If you look at the footage here, clearly a dash cam, he's explaining the situation to us, we can pause, get the registration and follow up and its numerous vehicles so what happens is the freeway units will be dispatched to the area.

VO: The initiative is barely 2 weeks old and the City of Joburg has already had over one thousand submissions. Member of the Mayoral Committee for Public Safety, Michael Sun has high hopes for this pilot project.

Michael: For so long we see our motorists and residents have been taken out their anger and frustration to social media, complaints of reckless driving, inconsiderate driving. The problem is that there are legal challenges why we can’t use this evidence in the past. We thought we really need to do something about this. Why not for us to set up our own platform.This is why are we are called Buya Mthetho hotline, its bring back the law.

VO: And bringing back the law it is, the hotline’s functions have expanded beyond reckless driving, now people can also submit bylaw infringements.

Derek: Michael, a tweet from the city of joburg, when you see reckless driving, move to the side and record or take a picture. That’s not going to happen surely*

Michael: Believe it or not a lot of our residents don’t take videos from their cars. There are pedestrians, passengers and a lot of the motorists now have dash cams.

Cut to someone skipping red robot… use as beat and pacer into Layton.

LINK: This car is fully kitted out. 2 dash cams, 2 gopros, our own camera. We are armed and dangerous, ready to nab some reckless drivers.

VO: Layton Beard Spokesperson for the Automobile Association is skeptical about how road users will implement this call to action. He joined us on our surveillance drive.

Layton: I think the city of joburg has got to be applauded for doing something different. Where our concern comes in the mechanism used to deal with that.

Derek: Why?

Layton: As we've just seen there's a driver, he's in a bakkie and he's going through a red light. If I didn’t have the dashcams here now I would have to take my cell phone out while I’m driving myself and record it.

Derek: We didn’t know he was going to jump the light.

Layton: When you saw him approaching the yellow at the speed he as approaching i think you could have seen he was going to do that.

Derek: So this idea of getting out the car and recording on your cell phone doesn’t work unless you stay at an intersection and you want to zap motorists going through that red light.

Layton: That would mean you need to pull off and sit at the side of the road and do the job that the JMPD should be doing.

Shots of Ambulance vehicles

VO: With 14 050 road deaths recorded in 2017, South African drivers rate among some of the worst in the world. Despite a recent recruitment drive of 1500 trainees by the city, at present, Johannesburg only has 2000 JMPD officers for 4 million motorists who need policing.

Layton: We have done surveys and this comes back to the big problem, what type of a driver do you think you are 75% are saying i’m an excellent driver, i abide by the rules of the road, everyone else is wrong so there is a disconnect between that opinion and what we see in the statistics in terms of crashes.

(violation as a transition to.. next scene)
LINK: We're heading off on patrol with JMPD spokesperson Wayne Minnaar in a marked metro police car so let’s see how the Joburg motorists behave now.

Wayne: On a normal patrol you find motorists breaking the law on just about every stretch of road you'll get a motorist overtaking when it’s not safe, a motorist crossing a solid white line.

Derek: We've been amazed at how many transgressions we've seen in the last few days.

Wayne: That’s why we have so many accidents and fatalities.

speed up of driving quick break…

Derek: It's amazing the difference driving around in a marked car and an unmarked car. The behaviour changes.

Wayne: If there’s no cop around people break the rules.

VO: The system will also flag hotspots for the JMPD to deploy more officers to particular areas. During our drive we came across a road block, and stopped to talk to some motorists about the hotline.

Derek: What do you think of the new hotline

Carla: I think it’s a good thing as long as there's action taken from it

Derek: Have you got a dash cam

Carla: No I don’t

Derek: So you'll have to use your cell phone

Carla: Yes but you have to stop, a lot of the time you you're sitting in a sand still in traffic so it’s not a problem and the taxis hop the pavements so it’s something and you’re standing still, that’s exactly what we want to catch.

LINK: It’s a bold project by the city to improve our driving but surely it also opens the door to vigilante behavior by motorists and more incidents of road rage when we see a little brother filming us breaking the law

Marie: I think the big thing is that people are going to start using it for the wrong reasons. Im angry at my boyfriend.

Derek: Vengeance and retribution

Marie: Vengeance and also that people are going to break the law just to get us footage

VO: Back on the beat in our marked vehicle an unsuspecting motorist was breaking the law, changing lanes without indicating, repeatedly.

JMPD Officer: I’m gonna stop him.

Derek: Not indicating at all

Derek: At least they've got emergency flickers

Derek: You admit you were violating the traffic laws

Sibu: Yes I admit

Derek: There's a new hotline starting where you can submit video of other drivers committing a felony or driving recklessly.

Sibu: I think I’d be more cautious knowing I could be on video at any moment

Derek: That little brother is watching you

Sibu: Ja and I don’t wanna be on tv for violations


VO: Howard Dembovsky Chairperson of the Justice Project South Africa, an NGO which concerns itself with road traffic legislation and its enforcement, commends the city for this initiative.

Howard: It has been implemented in Limpopo and from what I've seen has had some success there as well.There are obviously a few things that have to be taken into account because it’s not just as simple as uploading video footage to that particular hotline.

Offenses are things that are very dangerous like driving under the influence of alcohol, driving at speeds in excess of 40km over the speed limit. Now reckless driving would have to be prosecuted in terms of the criminal procedure act in a court but they don’t want to stand in court and testify and face the person they're accusing and the success of this project will depend on whether people are prepared to testify in court

VO: The city wants to assess the impact of this pilot project all the way to the prosecuting authorities and test how effective the outcomes will be. But drivers making submissions need to be above reproach themselves.

Howard: We've seen footage of people saying I’m going to prove this person is speeding so they whip out their phone hold it on their steering wheel and drive behind that vehicle and show their speedometer, wow look at this he’s driving at 180, well guess what so are you.

VO: Many motorists blame taxis for breaking the law, but it seems they won’t hesitate to follow suit.

Derek: Here's the taxi

Howard: And here's the mom's taxi.

Derek: Look at them, against the traffic. Someone could come around the corner head on

Howard: Correct and if you think high speed is the only thing that causes injuries think again. Two vehicles traveling at the same speed towards one another, that impact is horrible trust me.

Derek: With the hotline do we all become deputies of the JMPD.

Michael: I would encourage our citizens to go out there, not become the deputy but become the sheriff to say I don’t want lawlessness in the city and on our roads.

Road shot transition

Derek: That’s a violation.. ah we’ve got him!

During our drive we came across a road block, and stopped to talk to some motorists about the hotline. Derek: What do you think of the new hotline Carla: I think it’s a good thing as long as there's action taken from it Derek: Have you got a dash cam Carla: No I don’t Derek: So you'll have to use your cell phone Carla: Yes but you have to stop, a lot of the time you you're sitting in a sand still in traffic so it’s not a problem and the taxis hop the pavements so it’s something and you’re standing still, that’s exactly what we want to catch. LINK: It’s a bold project by the city to improve our driving but surely it also opens the door to vigilante behavior by motorists and more incidents of road rage when we see a little brother filming us breaking the law Marie: I think the big thing is that people are going to start using it for the wrong reasons. Im angry at my boyfriend. Derek: Vengeance and retribution Marie: Vengeance and also that people are going to break the law just to get us footage VO: Back on the beat in our marked vehicle an unsuspecting motorist was breaking the law, changing lanes without indicating, repeatedly. JMPD Officer: I’m gonna stop him. Derek: Not indicating at all Derek: At least they've got emergency flickers Derek: You admit you were violating the traffic laws Sibu: Yes I admit Derek: There's a new hotline starting where you can submit video of other drivers committing a felony or driving recklessly. Sibu: I think I’d be more cautious knowing I could be on video at any moment Derek: That little brother is watching you Sibu: Ja and I don’t wanna be on tv for violations VO: Howard Dembovsky Chairperson of the Justice Project South Africa, an NGO which concerns itself with road traffic legislation and its enforcement, commends the city for this initiative. Howard: It has been implemented in Limpopo and from what I've seen has had some success there as well.There are obviously a few things that have to be taken into account because it’s not just as simple as uploading video footage to that particular hotline. Offenses are things that are very dangerous like driving under the influence of alcohol, driving at speeds in excess of 40km over the speed limit. Now reckless driving would have to be prosecuted in terms of the criminal procedure act in a court but they don’t want to stand in court and testify and face the person they're accusing and the success of this project will depend on whether people are prepared to testify in court VO: The city wants to assess the impact of this pilot project all the way to the prosecuting authorities and test how effective the outcomes will be. But drivers making submissions need to be above reproach themselves. Howard: We've seen footage of people saying I’m going to prove this person is speeding so they whip out their phone hold it on their steering wheel and drive behind that vehicle and show their speedometer, wow look at this he’s driving at 180, well guess what so are you. VO: Many motorists blame taxis for breaking the law, but it seems they won’t hesitate to follow suit. Derek: Here's the taxi Howard: And here's the mom's taxi. Derek: Look at them, against the traffic. Someone could come around the corner head on Howard: Correct and if you think high speed is the only thing that causes injuries think again. Two vehicles traveling at the same speed towards one another, that impact is horrible trust me. Derek: With the hotline do we all become deputies of the JMPD. Michael: I would encourage our citizens to go out there, not become the deputy but become the sheriff to say I don’t want lawlessness in the city and on our roads. Road shot transition Derek: That’s a violation.. ah we’ve got him!

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Reckless Drivers Beware! Little Brothers are watching you! The COJ has launched a Reckless Driving Hotline for residents to send video reports of incidents of bad driving, direct to the JMPD.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Next time you spot reckless driving on the road don’t you wish you could do something about it? The City of Joburg is giving this opportunity to Johannesburg residents with their new Hotline number for reporting reckless drivers on WhatsApp. But how much safer will our roads be if good citizen drivers are trying to react instantly on their phones to any case of bad driving?
metadata.Summary: Just in February this year, the JMPD managed to catch 541 drunk drivers, but is that just the tip of the iceberg? The City of Joburg certainly think so and Mayor Herman Mashaba launched a new scheme at the end of March to combat driving offences. This time the strategy is to involve Johannesburg citizens, drivers and pedestrians, in alerting the police to road related offences. In essence, the city has set up a “Reckless Driving Hotline” on WhatsApp, the Facebook owned messaging service.
metadata.Further information: “When you see reckless driving behaviour: STOP, move to the side then record or take a picture.” So tweeted @CityofJoburgZA on 27th March this year. The City of Joburg, the Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department and the Department of Community Safety have joined forces in a new anti-road-crime initiative which harnesses the immediacy of video over WhatsApp. They envisage, that on witnessing a dangerous driving incident, vigilant onlookers will take a video of the action, or copy a clip from their car’s dashcam, and send it to 081 470 6338. Many of us wish we could do something about road crimes, road rage being rife in Johannesburg. But how easy will it be to report to this hotline properly and safely? And how effective will the City act on the alerts? Carte Blanche looks at how practical it is for a witness of reckless behaviour on the roads to report such incidents to the Hotline. We will do our own demo test to show how practical or impractical the whole process is of pulling over in a safe place, taking a video and then sending it on WhatsApp. The JMPD in co-operation with the Department of Community Safety have developed a system for receiving the public’s alerts, reviewing them and reacting to those that provide enough information to follow up on. Michael Sun, MMC of The Department of Community Safety, will take us behind the scenes to the operation room and show us how it works. And we will go driving with JMPD spokesperson Wayne Minaar to view the project from the law enforcement perspective. The JMPD say that on successfully identifying the perpetrator of any such alert by the public, and deeming the incident serious enough to be unlawful, they will issue a traffic citation which will probably include a fine. If multiple crimes are detected in this manner do the courts have capacity for people who don’t come forward to pay the fines? With the backlog in an already overburdened justice system will these traffic offences ever be prosecuted? The Hotline scheme may also lead to other unwanted side-effects. Ironically, there is the potential for an increase in reckless behaviour on the roads… by people attempting to catch an offender in a haphazard or over-zealous way. There are also opportunities for malicious exploitation of the scheme. For instance, what if someone holding a grudge towards a neighbour or work colleague, decides to stalk that person with their dashcam or phone at the ready? Then proceed to repeatedly report them to the Hotline for any vaguely reckless behaviour they exhibit on the road? Even so, however impractical the reporting procedure may be, Cllr Michael Sun emphasises that one of the main ambitions for the project is that,i there are some successful prosecutions and drivers know someone may be watching them, then the Hotline could act as an effective deterrent to reckless driving.
